subdomain_title: Developing ML models using BigQuery ML or AutoML on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
question: A retail analytics team keeps three years of customer activity in BigQuery. The analysts know SQL but not Python. They need a churn classifier this week, and the data must not leave BigQuery. What should they do?
choice_a: Export the tables to Cloud Storage and train a custom TensorFlow model in a notebook.
choice_b: Train a logistic regression model with CREATE MODEL in BigQuery ML.
choice_c: Copy the data into Cloud SQL with Dataflow and train there.
choice_d: Train a k-means model in BigQuery ML.
explanation_a: This works, but it moves the data out of BigQuery and needs Python skills the team does not have.
explanation_b: BigQuery ML trains and evaluates the classifier with SQL, inside BigQuery. It fits the skills, the deadline and the data rule.
explanation_c: Cloud SQL has no built-in model training, and the copy breaks the rule that the data stays in BigQuery.
explanation_d: K-means clusters unlabeled rows. Churn is a labeled yes or no outcome, so it needs a classifier.

subdomain_title: Developing ML models using BigQuery ML or AutoML on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
question: You must forecast daily sales for 400 stores in BigQuery ML. Sales show weekly seasonality and holiday peaks. Which model type fits best?
choice_a: linear_reg on the date as a numeric feature.
choice_b: ARIMA_PLUS, with the store column as time_series_id_col.
choice_c: kmeans on the sales column.
choice_d: matrix_factorization on store and date.
explanation_a: A straight line over the date cannot capture weekly cycles or holiday effects.
explanation_b: ARIMA_PLUS models trend and seasonality, and with holiday_region set it also models holiday effects. time_series_id_col fits one series per store in a single statement.
explanation_c: Clustering groups similar rows. It does not predict future values.
explanation_d: Matrix factorization is for recommendations from user and item interactions, not for time series.

subdomain_title: Building AI solutions using Google Cloud AI APIs or foundational models
question: An accounts team receives 5,000 scanned supplier invoices a month. They need the supplier name, due date and total as structured fields. No one on the team builds ML models. What should you use?
choice_a: Cloud Vision label detection.
choice_b: The Document AI invoice parser.
choice_c: A custom CNN trained on labeled invoice images.
choice_d: Speech-to-Text on a voice reading of each invoice.
explanation_a: Label detection names objects in an image, such as 'document'. It does not extract invoice fields.
explanation_b: The invoice parser is a pretrained processor that returns fields such as supplier, due date and total. It needs no model training.
explanation_c: A custom model needs labeled data and ML skills, and it repeats work a pretrained processor already does.
explanation_d: This adds a manual step and a second error source. The input is already an image.

subdomain_title: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
question: A linear model uses annual income as a feature. Income is heavily right-skewed, with a few very large values. What is the best preprocessing step?
choice_a: One-hot encode income.
choice_b: Apply a log transform, then standardize.
choice_c: Drop the income feature.
choice_d: Replace income with random noise of the same mean.
explanation_a: Income is continuous. One-hot encoding creates a column per value and discards the order.
explanation_b: The log compresses the long tail, so a few large values no longer dominate. Standardizing then puts the feature on a common scale.
explanation_c: Income is likely predictive. Skew is a reason to transform it, not to drop it.
explanation_d: This destroys the signal in the feature.

subdomain_title: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
question: A neural recommendation model has a product_id feature with 120,000 distinct values. Which two approaches handle it well? (Choose two.)
choice_a: Learn an embedding for each product_id.
choice_b: Hash product_id into a fixed number of buckets.
choice_c: One-hot encode product_id into 120,000 columns.
choice_d: Cast product_id to an integer and feed it as a numeric value.
explanation_a: An embedding maps each ID to a small dense vector that is learned during training. It scales to many values and captures similarity.
explanation_b: Hashing bounds the vocabulary size and handles unseen IDs. A few collisions are the accepted cost.
explanation_c: This gives a huge, sparse input layer and learns nothing about how products relate.
explanation_d: This invents an order and a distance between IDs that mean nothing.

subdomain_title: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
question: A churn model scores 99% accuracy on validation but performs poorly in production. One feature, refund_issued_date, is only filled in after a customer has already left. What is the most likely fix?
choice_a: Use a larger model.
choice_b: Remove features that are not known at prediction time.
choice_c: Train for more epochs.
choice_d: Make the validation set larger.
explanation_a: Model size does not fix a feature that leaks the label.
explanation_b: refund_issued_date leaks the outcome. At prediction time it is empty, so the model learned a shortcut that production never sees.
explanation_c: More training learns the leak even more strongly.
explanation_d: A larger validation set built the same way still contains the leak.

subdomain_title: Model prototyping using notebooks (e.g., Agent Platform Workbench and Colab Enterprise)
question: Two data scientists run the same notebook and get different results, because their environments have different library versions. What is the most reliable fix?
choice_a: Run the notebook from a custom container image with pinned library versions.
choice_b: Restart the kernel before each run.
choice_c: Use a larger machine type.
choice_d: Clear all cell outputs before committing.
explanation_a: A shared image with pinned versions gives every run the same environment, so results can be reproduced.
explanation_b: A restart clears state but keeps the mismatched libraries.
explanation_c: Machine size does not change library versions.
explanation_d: This keeps diffs clean but does not align the environments.

question: Your team must be able to reproduce any past training run exactly. Which two items must you record for each run? (Choose two.)
choice_a: The code version, such as the git commit.
choice_b: The exact dataset version or snapshot used.
choice_c: Only the final evaluation metric.
choice_d: The hostname of the training machine.
explanation_a: Without the exact code, a rerun can silently differ.
explanation_b: Data changes over time. Without the snapshot, the same code trains on different data.
explanation_c: A metric describes the result, but it cannot recreate the run.
explanation_d: Hostnames are temporary and do not affect the result.

subdomain_title: Building models given the task considering cost, complexity, latency, and scalability
question: A field-inspection app must classify photos on phones with no network, in under 50 ms. Which approach fits?
choice_a: A large ensemble on a GPU-backed online endpoint.
choice_b: A compact model, such as a quantized MobileNet, running on the device.
choice_c: A nightly batch prediction job.
choice_d: A call to a hosted foundation model API.
explanation_a: This needs a network connection, which the phones do not have.
explanation_b: A small quantized model runs locally with low latency and needs no connection.
explanation_c: Batch jobs cannot answer a photo taken a moment ago.
explanation_d: This needs a network connection and adds remote latency.

question: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss starts rising after epoch 5. What should you do?
choice_a: Raise the learning rate.
choice_b: Add early stopping and regularization, such as dropout or L2.
choice_c: Remove the validation set to train on more data.
choice_d: Train for many more epochs.
explanation_a: A higher learning rate does not address the gap between training and validation.
explanation_b: The model is overfitting. Early stopping keeps the best epoch, and regularization narrows the gap.
explanation_c: Without validation you can no longer detect overfitting.
explanation_d: This makes the overfitting worse.

question: In a fraud dataset, only 0.5% of rows are fraud. The model predicts 'not fraud' for every row. Which two steps help? (Choose two.)
choice_a: Use class weights so that errors on fraud cost more.
choice_b: Oversample fraud rows in the training split only.
choice_c: Oversample fraud rows before the train and test split.
choice_d: Drop the fraud rows as outliers.
explanation_a: Weighting the rare class makes the model pay attention to it, with no change to the data.
explanation_b: Resampling after the split balances training and keeps the evaluation data honest.
explanation_c: Copies of the same rows land in both splits. That leaks data and inflates the test scores.
explanation_d: This removes the very class you need to detect.

question: You train a large transformer in JAX. It is dominated by dense matrix multiplications, and training will run for weeks. Cost per unit of performance matters most. Which hardware fits best?
choice_a: Cloud TPUs.
choice_b: A pool of general-purpose CPU VMs.
choice_c: A single small inference GPU.
choice_d: Cloud Run functions.
explanation_a: TPUs are built for large dense matrix operations, and JAX supports them natively. They are often the most cost-efficient choice at this scale.
explanation_b: CPUs are far slower on dense matrix multiplication at this scale.
explanation_c: One small GPU would take far too long, and its memory limits the model size.
explanation_d: Serverless functions have time and memory limits that do not suit weeks of training.

question: GPU utilization stays near 30% during training. Profiling shows the data loader is the bottleneck. What should you do first?
choice_a: Move to a larger GPU.
choice_b: Parallelize and prefetch the input pipeline, and read from sharded TFRecord files.
choice_c: Reduce the batch size to 1.
choice_d: Add more layers to the model.
explanation_a: A faster GPU will wait even longer for data.
explanation_b: Parallel reads, prefetching and sharded files keep the accelerator fed. This fixes the stated bottleneck.
explanation_c: Tiny batches lower GPU efficiency even more.
explanation_d: This raises the compute per step but leaves the input bottleneck unsolved.

question: Each night you must score 200 million rows stored in BigQuery. No one waits for the results until morning. Which serving approach fits?
choice_a: An online endpoint called once per row.
choice_b: A batch prediction job that reads from BigQuery and writes the results back.
choice_c: A function that scores each row as it is inserted.
choice_d: A streaming Dataflow job with a model on every worker.
explanation_a: Per-row online calls are slow and costly for 200 million rows, and no one needs low latency here.
explanation_b: Batch prediction is built for large offline scoring. It scales out and needs no endpoint running all day.
explanation_c: The rows already exist. Scoring them as a stream adds complexity for no gain.
explanation_d: This is possible, but it means more moving parts than a managed batch job for a nightly task.

question: Online predictions are worse than offline evaluation. You find that the serving code reimplements feature scaling slightly differently from training. What is the best long-term fix?
choice_a: Rewrite the serving code more carefully to match training.
choice_b: Put the preprocessing inside the exported model, for example with Keras preprocessing layers or tf.Transform.
choice_c: Skip preprocessing at serving time.
choice_d: Log the raw inputs and compare them weekly.
explanation_a: Two copies of the logic will drift apart again.
explanation_b: One shared transform runs in both training and serving, which removes the training-serving skew at its source.
explanation_c: The model expects scaled inputs, so raw values make predictions worse.
explanation_d: Logging helps you detect skew, but it does not prevent it.

question: An online prediction endpoint gets 10 times its normal traffic every day at lunchtime, and latency breaks the target. What should you change?
choice_a: Raise the minimum replica count, and set a maximum above it so the endpoint autoscales on utilization.
choice_b: Move to one very large replica.
choice_c: Switch to nightly batch prediction.
choice_d: Lower the client timeout.
explanation_a: Warm minimum replicas absorb the first burst. Autoscaling adds replicas as load rises, but only when the maximum is above the minimum.
explanation_b: A single replica is a single point of failure, and it still has a fixed capacity ceiling.
explanation_c: Users need answers during the day, so batch scoring does not fit.
explanation_d: This turns slow responses into errors. It adds no capacity.

question: You trained a new model version and want to release it with low risk. What should you do?
choice_a: Replace the current model in place.
choice_b: Deploy it to the same endpoint, send it 10% of traffic, then shift more as its metrics hold.
choice_c: Ask users to choose the version they prefer.
choice_d: Undeploy the old model first, then deploy the new one.
explanation_a: Every user gets the new version at once, with no quick way back.
explanation_b: A traffic split is a canary release. It limits the impact of a bad model and allows a quick rollback.
explanation_c: Users cannot judge model quality, and the results would be biased.
explanation_d: This causes downtime and removes the fallback.

question: A large model is served on a GPU endpoint, but steady traffic is only about five requests per minute. You need responses within 300 ms. How can you cut serving cost the most?
choice_a: Distill or quantize the model so that it serves on a CPU machine type within the latency target.
choice_b: Switch to batch prediction once a day.
choice_c: Add a second GPU replica for redundancy.
choice_d: Raise the autoscaling target to 95% utilization.
explanation_a: A smaller model on CPU removes the idle GPU cost. This works only if quality and latency still meet the target, so test both first.
explanation_b: Requests need answers within 300 ms, so a daily batch does not fit.
explanation_c: This doubles the cost of an endpoint that already sits mostly idle.
explanation_d: With one replica at low load, the target changes little. The GPU still costs the same while idle.

question: Your preprocessing, training and evaluation steps run by hand from notebooks. You need repeatable runs and a lineage of the artifacts each step produced. What should you do?
choice_a: Schedule the notebooks with cron on a VM.
choice_b: Define the steps as Kubeflow Pipelines components and run them on a managed pipelines service.
choice_c: Keep running the notebooks by hand, but write down each run in a document.
choice_d: Run a single script from Cloud Shell.
explanation_a: This repeats the steps, but it records no artifact lineage and has no step-level retries.
explanation_b: A pipeline makes each step a tracked component. Runs are repeatable, and their inputs, outputs and lineage are recorded. On Google Cloud, Agent Platform Pipelines runs Kubeflow Pipelines.
explanation_c: Manual steps and notes are error-prone and do not scale.
explanation_d: Cloud Shell sessions are temporary, and a script records no lineage.

question: You want retraining to start when the serving feature distribution drifts past a threshold, not on a fixed calendar. What should you build?
choice_a: Retrain every hour, whatever the data shows.
choice_b: A monitoring alert that publishes to Pub/Sub, which triggers a pipeline run.
choice_c: A weekly email asking an engineer to check the charts.
choice_d: Never retrain, and keep the first model forever.
explanation_a: This wastes compute and can push out models that are no better.
explanation_b: Model Monitoring can send its alerts to a Pub/Sub notification channel. Drift then starts the run, and the pipeline retrains with the same tested steps each time.
explanation_c: This is manual and slow, and it is easy to miss.
explanation_d: Data drift slowly lowers the quality of the model.

question: An automated pipeline retrains a model every week. Last week, a worse model reached production. What should you add?
choice_a: An evaluation step that deploys the new model only if it beats the current model on a fixed holdout set.
choice_b: Longer training on each run.
choice_c: Deletion of the previous model after each run.
choice_d: Skip evaluation to save time.
explanation_a: A quality gate compares the two models on the same data and stops a regression before deployment.
explanation_b: Training longer does not guarantee a better model, and it is no check.
explanation_c: This removes the fallback you need if the new model is worse.
explanation_d: This is how the worse model reached production in the first place.

question: Support chat transcripts used to fine-tune a model contain names, phone numbers and card numbers. What should you do before training?
choice_a: Train on the raw text and restrict who can access the model.
choice_b: De-identify the transcripts with Sensitive Data Protection.
choice_c: Remove every transcript that has a number in it.
choice_d: Encrypt the training files at rest.
explanation_a: Models can memorize and repeat personal data, so access rules alone do not protect it.
explanation_b: Sensitive Data Protection finds and masks or replaces personal data before the text reaches training.
explanation_c: This drops most of the useful data and still misses names.
explanation_d: Encryption protects the files in storage, but the model still learns the personal data.

question: A loan approval model has high overall accuracy. You must check whether it treats applicant groups unfairly. What should you do?
choice_a: Rely on the overall accuracy number.
choice_b: Compute evaluation metrics separately for each relevant group and compare them.
choice_c: Remove the group attribute and treat the model as fair.
choice_d: Retrain with a different random seed.
explanation_a: An overall metric can hide large differences between groups.
explanation_b: Sliced metrics, such as false negative rate per group, show whether some groups are served worse.
explanation_c: Other features can stand in for the removed attribute, so bias can remain.
explanation_d: A new seed does not measure fairness or address it.

subdomain_title: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions
question: Production accuracy has dropped over two months. Labels arrive with a long delay. How can you detect the problem early?
choice_a: Wait for the labels, then recompute accuracy.
choice_b: Monitor serving features for skew from the training data and for drift over time, and alert past a threshold.
choice_c: Retrain on the original training data.
choice_d: Turn off logging to reduce latency.
explanation_a: This finds the problem only months late.
explanation_b: Skew and drift detection need no labels, so they warn early that the model may be degrading.
explanation_c: Training on the same old data does not address a shift in the inputs.
explanation_d: Without logs you cannot observe drift at all.

subdomain_title: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions
question: A customer asks why the model rejected their application. What helps you explain that single prediction?
choice_a: Global feature importance from the training run.
choice_b: Per-prediction feature attributions, such as SHAP or integrated gradients.
choice_c: The model's accuracy on the test set.
choice_d: The model's architecture diagram.
explanation_a: Global importance describes the model on average, not this one decision.
explanation_b: Local attributions show how each feature of this input pushed the score up or down. Sampled Shapley and integrated gradients are two common methods.
explanation_c: Accuracy describes overall quality, not the reasons for one case.
explanation_d: The structure of the model does not explain a specific prediction.
